::: {#thm-infinitely-many-primes}
#### There are infinitely many primes

There are infinitely many prime numbers (@def-prime)
[@wikipedia_euclids_theorem].

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: proof

Suppose, for contradiction, that there are only finitely many primes,
and list them all as $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k$.
The list is not empty, because $2$ is prime.
Let

$$
N = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k + 1.
$$

Each $p_i \ge 2$, so $N \ge 3$,
and by @rem-prime-divisor some prime $p$ divides $N$: $N = p s$ for some integer $s$.
The list holds every prime, so $p$ is one of $p_1, \ldots, p_k$,
and so $p$ also divides their product: $p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k = p t$ for some integer $t$. Then

$$
\ba
1
&= N - p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k
&& \text{(definition of } N \text{)}
\\&= p s - p t
&& \text{(substitute both products)}
\\&= p (s - t).
&& \text{(distributive law, read from right to left)}
\ea
$$

Since $s - t$ is an integer (@rem-integer-closure), $p \mid 1$.
But $p \ge 2$, and $p \cd 0 = 0 < 1 < p = p \cd 1$,
so no integer $c$ has $p c = 1$, and $p \nmid 1$.
That is a contradiction,
so there are infinitely many primes.

:::

:::
